prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for the optical lattice clock (B008), credited to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements and the chair's questions, the scientific case has not weakened, and the exchange has sharpened it. Six members reach it from different directions: atomic structure (Lindroth), laser metrology (Kroll), astroparticle and instrumentation (Pearce), electron microscopy (Olsson) and circuit physics (Johansson). None found a flaw in the physics. The distinctness question is the one that matters, so I will answer it directly. The 2005 prize honoured comb-based optical frequency measurement and the 2012 prize honoured control of individual quantum systems. The lattice clock is neither. Its new content is the magic-wavelength condition, which makes the trapping light shift the two clock levels equally. That lets a large ensemble be held tightly enough to remove Doppler and recoil shifts, without perturbing the transition, while many atoms are interrogated at once. That architecture is what moved optical clocks from the 1e-15 regime to about 1e-18, and it has been reproduced in Sr, Yb and Hg. Single-ion clocks cannot take that route, because their statistics are limited by one particle. For the chair's wording question, I would keep the citation as it stands, 'for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock'. It names the lattice architecture, so it cannot be read as a prize for precision timekeeping in general, and it says nothing about the redefinition of the second. On attribution, Katori carries the concept and the first demonstrations and Ye carries the record accuracy and the many-body-enhanced operation. I accept that this is a judgement, but it is a defensible one, and I would not widen it to settle priority questions.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is still that the lattice clock is a brilliant refinement of work already honoured in 2005 and 2012, and that Ye in particular comes out of the comb and ultrastable-laser tradition. I think the lattice-architecture argument answers this, but a sceptical Academy member will press it, and the citation has to carry that argument. A second objection is the credit outside the two names, because NIST, PTB, SYRTE and the Tokyo group all contributed. A third is timing, since the redefinition of the second is pending; I regard that as neutral to mildly favourable and not a reason to wait, because the committee's criterion is the invention and not its regulatory adoption. Against my own round-1 sympathies, I also have to weigh the Higgs discovery (B056). Its scientific stature is larger than that of the clock, and I have not stopped thinking so. But I cannot write a defensible three-name allocation from four credited people inside two collaborations, and I will not add it as a second part merely to compensate for that difficulty. A two-part prize needs two cases that each stand alone, and I have not seen a second case here that does.

responses.point: Kroll reports finding no second shortlisted candidate that is stronger than the clock alone, and judges the lattice clock distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, while disclosing a research stay in Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: I agree that a two-part pairing would dilute the clock and I now say so explicitly: I have found no second part that stands on its own. On distinctness, I accept your framing that the citation must rest on the lattice concept, and I have tried to supply the scientific reason in this round: many-atom, Doppler- and recoil-free interrogation through the magic wavelength, which single-ion control cannot supply. On your disclosure, I think the Hall stay and the laser-stabilisation work are exactly the experience that makes your technical assessment valuable. I would record it in the minutes and apply no discount, because Hall's own prize is a precedent that we are all reading and not a stake in Katori or Ye.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers trapped-ion quantum logic (B022, Cirac, Zoller, Blatt) as an original, three-decade line from proposal to realisation, concedes that Wineland and Monroe weaken the experimental share, and names B008 as the more compact and less disputed prize if those points are not resolved.
responses.response: I respect the Cirac-Zoller proposal as an original idea, and I agree that the criterion concerns the invention and not whether scalable quantum computing has arrived. But you have identified the weakness yourself. The first experimental gate came from Wineland's group, whose work is already covered by the 2012 prize, and the Blatt allocation is a judgement call that Pearce and Kroll also press. You also observe that the overlap argument applies to B008 too. I think it applies less strongly, because the lattice clock rests on a different mechanism from the ion-control work, whereas trapped-ion gates sit directly on it. If the committee cannot settle the Blatt question, which I do not think it can from the evidence supplied, then your own fallback to B008 is the right outcome, and I would welcome your support for it.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers twisted bilayer graphene (B035) as a case in which a quantitative prediction preceded a decisive experiment, argues that a prize can precede a settled mechanism, and holds that B008 is mainly a large precision gain that does not change our understanding of matter in the way a tunable correlated platform does.
responses.response: The prediction-then-discovery structure is a real strength and I do not dismiss it. I disagree that the lattice clock is only a precision gain. It is a new measuring instrument, and the 1e-18 regime brings in physics that was not accessible before: clock comparisons that are sensitive to gravitational redshift over centimetres, bounds on drifts of fundamental constants, and many-body effects in the clock ensemble itself. That is a change in what we can ask of nature, which is where I would put the weight. On B035, your own concession matters more than my objection. The origin of the superconductivity is still debated, Cao and other experimentalists lie outside the three names, and the committee's habit is to wait while the interpretation is moving. If the mechanism and the experimental credit were settled in a few years, I would take the case seriously. I do not think it is ready now, and I would not move your configuration into a two-part prize on that basis.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, treats B008 as having a concrete before-and-after and no real maturity question, and ranks IceCube (B042) as the second alternative, with the allocation among IceCube, AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND unresolved.
responses.response: We agree on the lead. On your question about Ye and the 2005 prize, I think the comb is a tool he used and not the lattice clock itself, so the overlap lowers his standing less than it might seem. I still read the result as an experimental programme in its own right: the record accuracy and many-body operation were achieved with the lattice architecture. I accept your point that IceCube's source identification is still modest in significance, so it is not ready this year. My own second alternative is the Higgs discovery rather than IceCube, for the reason I gave in round 1 and which you share. I would still add that the attribution problem is a problem of the three-name limit and not of the discovery, and that this does not bear on B008.

responses.point: Olsson ranks B008 second behind her field-adjacent B009 (aberration correction), holds that B009 is a mature invention but has a credit problem with Krivanek, and says she would consider recusal on B009.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour about your field loyalty and I think the recusal reasoning is sound for B009 and not needed for B008. It also answers the chair's question about discounting: no one with a disclosed tie to a candidate needs to be excluded from the B008 decision, so I do not see a case for recusal there. On the substance, I still think the Krivanek and independent STEM corrector questions make B009 harder to defend than a two-name clock prize, so I agree that B008 is the better configuration this year. I would only add that your own listing of B009 as an alternative keeps it available for the future. I also agree with you that the pending redefinition of the second is neutral rather than a reason to defer.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice architecture, with magic-wavelength trapping and parallel many-atom interrogation, as the distinguishing invention relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.

Exact priority between Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock demonstrations, and the weight of NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other groups; I recall this from memory and cannot verify it from the supplied files.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second should be treated as a reason to wait, to proceed, or as irrelevant to the committee's criterion; I lean towards irrelevant.
Whether the Higgs discovery (B056) deserves a place in a later year despite the three-name allocation problem, and whether a future two-part prize with it would be defensible.
statement.conflict_note: No change. No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile: my documented connections are David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theory group, and none is connected to Katori, Ye or the named alternatives. I note that I am a string theorist and cosmologist, so I judge the atomic physics of the clock partly on the arguments of Lindroth and Kroll and not on my own expertise. I see no basis for recusal of any member on B008, and I would record the disclosures of Kroll and Pearce in the minutes without applying a discount.
